young.what: Your skull is the bony helmet inside your head.
young.does: It keeps your brain safe and gives your face its shape.
young.funFact: A baby's skull has soft spots that slowly close up as the baby grows!

junior.what: The skull is the bony framework of the head: cranial bones around the brain and facial bones at the front.
junior.does: The cranium protects the brain, while the facial bones support the eyes, nose and teeth and give the chewing muscles somewhere to attach.
junior.funFact: Most skull bones are joined by wiggly seams called sutures, which lock them together like puzzle pieces.
junior.details: The skull has 22 bones: 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones. Only the lower jaw can move freely.

young.what: Your jaw bone is the bone of your chin that holds your bottom teeth.
young.does: It moves up and down so you can chew, talk and sing.
young.funFact: Your jaw bone is the only bone in your skull that you can move!

junior.what: The mandible is the U-shaped bone of the lower jaw.
junior.does: Strong chewing muscles pull it up to bite, and it can also slide from side to side to grind food.
junior.funFact: The mandible is the largest and strongest bone of the face.
junior.details: It holds the lower teeth and joins the skull at the jaw joint, just in front of each ear.

young.what: Your backbone is a tall stack of small bones down the middle of your back.
young.does: It holds you up straight and lets you bend and twist.
young.funFact: It is made of lots of small bones called vertebrae, stacked like building blocks!

junior.what: The vertebral column, or spine, is a flexible column of bones called vertebrae running from the skull to the pelvis.
junior.does: It supports the head and body, protects the spinal cord inside it, and lets you bend and twist. Soft discs between the vertebrae work as shock absorbers.
junior.funFact: A baby has 33 vertebrae, but some join together while growing up, so an adult has 26.
junior.details: From top to bottom there are 7 neck (cervical), 12 chest (thoracic) and 5 lower-back (lumbar) vertebrae, then the sacrum and coccyx.

young.what: Your ribs are curved bones that wrap around your chest like a cage.
young.does: They protect your heart and lungs and move when you breathe.
young.funFact: Most people have 12 pairs of ribs. That's 24 ribs!

junior.what: The rib cage is made of 12 pairs of ribs, joined to the thoracic vertebrae at the back and, for most ribs, to the breastbone at the front.
junior.does: It protects the heart and lungs. Muscles between the ribs lift them when you breathe in, making the chest bigger.
junior.funFact: The lowest two pairs are called 'floating ribs' because they are not attached to the breastbone.
junior.details: Pairs 1–7 join the breastbone directly by cartilage (true ribs). Pairs 8–10 join through the cartilage of the rib above (false ribs). Pairs 11–12 float free at the front.

young.what: Your breastbone is a flat bone in the middle of your chest.
young.does: Your ribs join onto it to make a strong shield for your heart.
young.funFact: Press gently in the middle of your chest and you can feel your breastbone!

junior.what: The sternum is a flat, dagger-shaped bone at the front of the chest.
junior.does: It anchors the ribs through strips of cartilage and helps protect the heart.
junior.funFact: It has three parts: the manubrium (handle), the body (blade) and the xiphoid process (tip).
junior.details: The collarbones join the top of the sternum, linking your arms to the chest skeleton.

young.what: Your collarbones are two thin bones across the top of your chest.
young.does: They hold your shoulders out to the sides so your arms can move freely.
young.funFact: You can feel your collarbone just under the skin near your neck!

junior.what: The clavicle is a long, S-shaped bone between the breastbone and the shoulder blade.
junior.does: It works like a strut, holding the shoulder away from the body and passing forces from the arm to the trunk.
junior.funFact: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to start hardening before birth.
junior.details: Together, the clavicle and the scapula form the pectoral (shoulder) girdle.

young.what: Your shoulder blades are two flat, triangle-shaped bones on your upper back.
young.does: They help your arms swing, reach and lift.
young.funFact: Your shoulder blades slide around on your back when you move your arms!

junior.what: The scapula is a large, flat, triangular bone on the upper back, lying over the 2nd to 7th ribs.
junior.does: Its shallow glenoid cavity forms the shoulder joint with the humerus, and many shoulder and back muscles attach to it.
junior.funFact: The scapula is held in place mostly by muscles rather than joints, which is why the shoulder can move so freely.
junior.details: A ridge on its back, the spine of the scapula, ends in the acromion, the bony tip of your shoulder.

young.what: This is the bone inside the top part of your arm.
young.does: It helps you lift and swing your arm.
young.funFact: The tingly 'funny bone' feeling happens near the bottom end of this bone!

junior.what: The humerus is the long bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow.
junior.does: Its rounded head fits into the shoulder blade to make a ball-and-socket joint, and its lower end forms the elbow's hinge joint with the radius and ulna.
junior.funFact: The 'funny bone' feeling comes from bumping the ulnar nerve where it passes the humerus at the elbow.
junior.details: The deltoid, biceps and triceps muscles all attach to the humerus.

young.what: The radius is one of two bones in your forearm, on the thumb side.
young.does: It lets you turn your hand over, palm up and palm down.
young.funFact: When you turn a doorknob, your radius rolls around the other forearm bone!

junior.what: The radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side.
junior.does: It rotates around the ulna so you can turn your palm up (supination) and down (pronation).
junior.funFact: The radius is the forearm bone that is most often broken, usually by falling onto an outstretched hand.
junior.details: At the wrist, the radius joins the carpal bones, so it carries most of the load from the hand.

young.what: The ulna is the other forearm bone, on the little-finger side.
young.does: It makes the hinge of your elbow with your upper arm bone.
young.funFact: The pointy bump of your elbow is the top of your ulna!

junior.what: The ulna is the forearm bone on the little-finger side.
junior.does: Its hook-shaped top wraps around the humerus to form the elbow's hinge joint, and it stays still while the radius rotates.
junior.funFact: The point of your elbow is a part of the ulna called the olecranon.
junior.details: The triceps muscle attaches to the olecranon and pulls on it to straighten the arm.

young.what: Your hand has lots of small bones in the wrist, palm and fingers.
young.does: They let your hand bend in many places so you can grip and wiggle.
young.funFact: Each hand has 27 bones. More than a quarter of all your bones are in your hands!

junior.what: The hand skeleton has 27 bones: 8 carpals in the wrist, 5 metacarpals in the palm and 14 phalanges in the fingers.
junior.does: Many small bones linked by movable joints make the hand flexible enough for writing, gripping and other fine movements.
junior.funFact: Your hands and feet together contain more than half of all the bones in your body.
junior.details: The thumb has only 2 phalanges; each of the other fingers has 3.

young.what: Your hip bones make a strong bowl shape at the bottom of your tummy.
young.does: They hold up the top half of your body and join onto your legs.
young.funFact: Put your hands on your hips and you are touching the top of your pelvis!

junior.what: The pelvis is a ring of bones made of two hip bones joined at the front and the sacrum at the back.
junior.does: It carries the weight of the upper body to the legs, protects organs such as the bladder, and forms the hip joints.
junior.funFact: Each hip bone starts as three separate bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse together as you grow.
junior.details: A deep cup on each side, the acetabulum, holds the ball-shaped head of the femur.

young.what: Your thigh bone is the long bone in the top part of your leg.
young.does: It holds up your body when you stand, walk and jump.
young.funFact: It is the longest and strongest bone in your whole body!

junior.what: The femur is the bone of the thigh, running from the hip to the knee.
junior.does: Its ball-shaped head fits into the pelvis at the hip, and its lower end forms the knee joint with the tibia.
junior.funFact: Your femur is roughly a quarter of your height.
junior.details: Inside the femur is bone marrow, which makes new blood cells.

young.what: Your kneecap is a small, round bone at the front of your knee.
young.does: It protects your knee and helps your leg straighten.
young.funFact: Babies' kneecaps are made of soft cartilage and slowly turn into bone!

junior.what: The patella is a small, triangular bone at the front of the knee joint.
junior.does: It sits inside the tendon of the quadriceps muscle and works like a pulley, making it easier to straighten the knee.
junior.funFact: The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, a type of bone that grows inside a tendon.
junior.details: Strong ligaments inside the knee, such as the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), hold the femur and tibia together.

young.what: Your shin bone is the big bone at the front of your lower leg.
young.does: It carries your weight from your knee down to your ankle.
young.funFact: You can feel your shin bone right under the skin at the front of your leg!

junior.what: The tibia is the larger, inner bone of the lower leg.
junior.does: It carries almost all of the body's weight between the knee and the ankle.
junior.funFact: The tibia is the second-longest bone in the body, after the femur.
junior.details: The bump on the inside of your ankle is the lower end of the tibia.

young.what: The fibula is a thin bone on the outside of your lower leg.
young.does: It helps keep your ankle steady and gives muscles a place to hold on.
young.funFact: It is much thinner than the shin bone right next to it!

junior.what: The fibula is the thin, outer bone of the lower leg.
junior.does: It carries little of the body's weight but anchors leg muscles and helps form the ankle joint.
junior.funFact: The bump on the outside of your ankle is the lower end of the fibula.
junior.details: Because it carries so little weight, surgeons sometimes use a piece of the fibula to repair other bones.

young.what: Your foot has lots of small bones in the ankle, the middle of the foot and the toes.
young.does: They work together to balance you and push you forward when you walk.

junior.what: The foot skeleton has 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges.
junior.does: The bones form arches that spread your weight and act like springs when you walk, run and jump.
junior.funFact: The calcaneus, or heel bone, is the largest bone in the foot.
junior.details: The talus sits on top of the heel bone and forms the ankle joint with the tibia and fibula.
